title: AI Market Domination and the Natural Monopoly Problem
author: Tejas Narechania

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess legal AI primarily through task-level capability, verification or legal-work redesign. It redirects attention to upstream model-market concentration, arguing that economies of scale, infrastructure control and vertical integration require competition rules, shared compute and early regulatory intervention. Its use-case and auditing concerns are compatible with selective deployment, but they are secondary to this materially different market-structure framing.
qs: But what there's not uncertainty about is there are huge economies of scale and that this is a market that tends towards some degree of concentration, whether it's one provider or just a handful.

That's something to think about, I think, is what are the rules that we want in order to ensure fair competition amongst applications and prevent a less good application from winning the market simply by virtue of the fact of being affiliated with GPT rather than actually being created by the best engineers.

st.t: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
st.an: The source accepts that scale and investment pressures are likely to concentrate AI development without making monopoly inevitable. It materially extends the proposition by predicting oligopoly, distinguishing model-layer concentration from application-layer competition, and framing shared infrastructure and public-interest policy as ways to capture scale efficiencies while limiting concentrated power.
qs: Again, we're not confident yet that this is going to be an natural monopoly in the same sense as telecom, but you make an interesting point.
And even if we're not confident that every one of these is a natural monopoly, I think we're pretty sure that all of these is some form of a natural oligopoly.

kp.k: Foundation-model economics may favour natural monopoly
kp.d: Narechania argues that some AI and machine-learning markets resemble natural monopolies because building underlying models requires substantial fixed investment in compute, data, energy and engineering. His argument concerns model development rather than applications built on models. Drawing on telephone networks, he frames the trade-off as duplicative infrastructure under competition versus pricing power and weak service incentives under monopoly.
qs: I should be super clear here that what I'm talking about are building the underlying models, building GPT-4, not building some application that sits on top of GPT-4.
The fixed costs of building machine learning or AI systems are really, really high.
And so the idea is that the market is naturally most efficient if it's served by a monopolist.

kp.k: User feedback could reinforce incumbent model advantages
kp.d: Narechania proposes a scale-feedback mechanism: resource-rich developers build models, attract users, improve models through downstream use and attract further users. He argues that fragmentation could distribute learning across competing models and reduce aggregate quality gains. This is presented as a theoretical mechanism for some models, not a measured finding about learning rates.
qs: You attract users to the model, it gets smarter based on those users. So then more users will come to that model and so on.
There's this sort of virtuous circle scale effect for some of these models.
if you have several different LLMs or if you have several different models, then what happens is that that learning is distributed and no one model learns best.

kp.k: Natural monopoly remains conditional on market boundaries
kp.d: Narechania distinguishes market-wide economies of scale from ordinary manufacturing scale economies. He acknowledges that scale benefits may run out, specialised use cases may require different models, and geographic market definitions remain uncertain. Nevertheless, he asserts that large fixed costs and network effects favour concentration among one or a few providers; the transcript supplies no empirical market test establishing natural monopoly.
qs: one of the traditional definitions of a natural monopoly is that the benefits of scale extend throughout the entire market.
reasonable people could disagree over whether or not every single model development use case is in fact a natural monopoly.

It might be that your benefits of skill run out at some point, or it might be that certain models are best deployed for particular use cases, and that's a narrow market, and then you want a different model for a different set of use cases.
even if we're not confident that every one of these is a natural monopoly, I think we're pretty sure that all of these is some form of a natural oligopoly.

kp.k: Utility regulation offers an alternative to conventional antitrust
kp.d: Narechania contrasts regulation of markets most efficiently served by few providers with antitrust intervention in markets that could sustain competition. In the former, permission to serve the market is exchanged for rate and service obligations. For AI, he recommends considering monetary charges, user data extraction and minimum service quality rather than assuming market concentration alone delivers public benefits.
qs: In exchange for that, you promise to comply with certain conditions.
You promise to comply with certain rate conditions so you don't charge monopoly prices.

So we regulate in order to prevent them from charging monopoly prices, that is, to try to approximate the prices that they would charge in a competitive market, and to make sure that they meet some minimum quality standards.

kp.k: AI pricing oversight should protect continued development
kp.d: Narechania treats both per-token API fees and privacy costs as possible subjects of rate regulation. He explicitly declines to confirm the host's suggestion that developer access is loss-making. He argues that permitted charges and data collection rules should accommodate investment in subsequent models while constraining what data is collected, under which conditions and for which purposes. These are proposals about AI input costs, not law-firm billing practices.
qs: They pay on a per-token basis. And so you might be worried about how much that cost is, and you may wish to regulate or scrutinize those costs.
So one form of rate regulation you might think about is data rate regulation.
I don't know the extent to which they are operating at a loss when they charge developers to access the model through their APIs, for example.
what we do or what we allow the model builder to charge should include the ability to do continued development.

kp.k: Model-level bias warrants quality standards and audits
kp.d: Narechania argues that biased training data can embed discrimination in models, with applications transmitting it despite possible mitigation through fine-tuning. He recommends predeployment audits and quality standards across racial, gender and linguistic groups. Hiring discrimination and unequal facial-recognition performance in criminal contexts illustrate his concerns; he also suggests competition might partly improve these quality dimensions, rather than claiming it would eliminate discrimination.
qs: I think the discrimination is in the model, and the application is the conduit between what the model thinks is the right or the wrong answer and the user.
It may be that some applications can fine tune the model a little bit or do something to try to mitigate some of those effects
you maybe want that quality standard to be across races, across genders, across linguistic backgrounds, and you could audit the systems for that before they're deployed in the real world.
we might be able to improve some of our concern, address in part some of our concerns on bias and discrimination in models, if we had more competition.

kp.k: Concentration creates cascading infrastructure and model risks
kp.d: Narechania describes a concentrated stack linking applications, models, cloud infrastructure and chips, where failures or security vulnerabilities can propagate upward. He uses hypothetical GPT outages, chip-supply interruptions and flawed medical models to illustrate systemic exposure. In the chip scenario, existing infrastructure would initially remain but growth and eventual replacement would be threatened. These are risk arguments, not reported incidents or quantified forecasts.
qs: If you have a lot of applications that are built on GPT and if GPT goes down, then all of a sudden, a whole range of services will become inoperable for as long as GPT is down.
It's a stack of concentration.
So if you were unable to get new chips, I think, you know, the infrastructure we have would continue, would exist until it fails and you need to replace it.
An error in that concentrated ecosystem could be hugely problematic because there's only one model, and you've got a rush to get it out, and turns out it's wrong.

kp.k: Early intervention could prevent political entrenchment
kp.d: Narechania recommends acting before further consolidation, arguing that established firms acquire political power to block regulation and become difficult to dislodge. He acknowledges that regulation could marginally slow technological development but could also prevent harmful deployment. His preference rests partly on greater trust in electoral accountability than in entrenched private providers; it is a normative judgment, not an empirical comparison of governance outcomes.
qs: Because once the industry has developed, frankly, it has more political power to delay, to block, propose regulation.
It's possible that maybe regulation will have some adverse effect on the development of the technology on the margins.
If the regulator gets it wrong, if the policy makers get it wrong, we can vote them out.
I think waiting for the market to consolidate further is not a good idea.

kp.k: Self-preferencing could distort competition in legal AI applications
kp.d: Narechania warns that model providers could favour affiliated chat or contract-drafting applications through preferential prices or advance access to models. This could allow an inferior application to win through affiliation rather than engineering quality. He extends the concern to cloud providers favouring associated models, drawing analogies to Apple, Microsoft antitrust and net-neutrality disputes. These are prospective competitive mechanisms, not findings of misconduct by a named legal-AI provider.
qs: a model builder might have their own chat application or their own contract drafting application.
Might give favorable pricing terms to their own application or they might give that one advance access to the next model.
it might be that the affiliated applications have a leg up and that distorts competition amongst applications.
prevent a less good application from winning the market simply by virtue of the fact of being affiliated with GPT rather than actually being created by the best engineers.

kp.k: Nondiscrimination and separation could protect downstream competition
kp.d: Narechania proposes equal pricing and access to advanced models for applications, or stronger structural separation between model and application businesses. When Cohen illustrates separation with AI Lawyer and legal-drafting tools, Narechania endorses having a separate corporate entity build the application. These are proposed market-structure rules, not existing legal-profession ownership or professional-conduct requirements.
qs: So you can imagine non-discrimination rules here, which is treat all the applications the same. Price them the same, give them equal access to advanced models.
Or you could go even further and have a sort of structural separation rule, which is if you operate in two markets, you have to have two different companies.
Yeah, so I think you would have to offer applications as a separate entity from the model.
Right, you would have to be some separate, and some separate corporate entity that's building the AI Lawyer, the AI Copywriter, the AI, whatever.

kp.k: Public compute could lower model-entry barriers
kp.d: Narechania advocates considering public options at different layers, especially publicly owned computational infrastructure available to competing model builders. His mechanism is to reduce capital constraints and make model markets more capable of sustaining price and quality competition. Responding to government-capacity concerns, he invokes the internet's origins as a government research project and public infrastructure analogies. He describes national AI resource discussions as a potentially attainable policy avenue, without a specific implementation timetable.
qs: a publicly owned computational infrastructure that is available for other people to use and other would-be competitors to use and build competing models.

they don't face those huge capital constraints and the market looks less like a natural monopoly market and more like one that can sustain competition and give us the good benefits of competition, price and quality competition.
There have been some discussions about building national AI resource.

kp.k: Public training datasets require privacy and compensation safeguards
kp.d: Narechania suggests public data repositories could help initiate model training but stresses unresolved design questions about inclusion, privacy and contributor compensation. Cohen raises compensating citizens and copyright holders; Narechania accepts the possibility without offering a settled mechanism. He points to existing data.gov repositories as examples of public data potentially usable for training.
qs: Maybe in some contexts, a public option for data makes a lot of sense, which is let's create a public repository of data that could be used to help start model training.
I think that's controversial and I think that that requires a lot of care and thought because of the privacy implications.
I think those are tricky questions, and I don't have all the answers for those, but I think there's a lot of room for policy creativity in that space.
If you go to data.gov, there are huge repositories of really interesting public data that already exist and could be used to train models on traffic, for example.

kp.k: Interoperability could combine shared scale with application competition
kp.d: Using the 1996 Telecommunications Act as an analogy, Narechania proposes infrastructure-sharing obligations, including equal Azure terms for rival model builders and OpenAI. He also proposes federated learning through a shared model to preserve learning benefits across applications. In that arrangement, competition would shift from model intelligence toward application usability and experience. He argues that reduced duplicative compute investment and carbon costs could justify intervention despite provider opposition; these are proposed benefits rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: these rules required AT&T to share their network with would-be competitors.
Microsoft to share its infrastructure with its Azure infrastructure with other model builders on terms equal to that which it provides it to open AI.
you could create a federated learning model where what you do is have a single shared model that learns from across applications.
So you get different degrees of differentiation at the application layer rather than at the model layer.
If we are more efficient at model building and we get competition in the application, well, that's good for us.

kp.k: Near-term priorities target quality, privacy and platform power
kp.d: Asked about likely early regulation, Narechania identifies service standards, privacy and data-collection rules, and restrictions on infrastructure or model providers favouring their own products as attainable priorities. He frames these primarily as recommendations that could curb corporate power, not firm predictions of enactment. Public computational infrastructure is also described as reachable, though less immediately attainable.
qs: I think we need to have some service standards in place.
I think we probably need some sort of privacy and data collection regulation in place.
I think we need rules that prevent entities that own either the computational infrastructure or that build models from self-preferencing their own models and applications.
investing in a public computational infrastructure for would-be competitors is also maybe not the lowest hanging fruit, but low enough that we could reach it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Narechania argues that foundation-model development tends toward concentration because of substantial fixed costs and reinforcing scale effects, while qualifying whether it constitutes a natural monopoly in every market.
pts.d: This is principally a cross-domain argument about AI infrastructure and markets, not a prediction about lawyers' employment or productivity. Narechania distinguishes building underlying models from building applications on them. He argues that compute, energy, data and engineering costs create entry barriers, and that learning from downstream use can strengthen leading models. A single model could reduce duplicated investment and aggregate learning, but concentration creates risks of monopoly pricing and weaker service-quality incentives. He expresses greater confidence in concentration among a few providers than in universal single-provider monopoly.

pts.k: Narechania claims that concentration can propagate model bias and amplify failures across applications and infrastructure.
pts.d: He locates much discriminatory behavior in the underlying model rather than solely in the application, while allowing that applications can mitigate it. He argues that competition could partly improve incentives to address bias. Separately, he describes concentrated dependencies across applications, models, clouds and chips as sources of systemic fragility: model outages can disable many services, chip disruptions can halt expansion, and a flawed widely deployed medical model could spread errors. These are mechanisms and conditional scenarios, not reported incidents or measured probabilities.

pts.k: Narechania predicts that vertically integrated model providers could distort competition among applications, including contract-drafting tools, through preferential access and pricing.
pts.d: His legal-market-specific example is a model builder favoring its own contract-drafting application. He describes this as a possibility rather than documenting an actual instance. Better pricing or earlier access to new models could let an affiliated application prevail over a better independent competitor. He proposes nondiscrimination rules or structural separation between model and application businesses, and extends the same concern to relationships between cloud providers and model developers.

pts.k: Narechania argues that public infrastructure and interoperability could lower entry barriers and preserve shared scale benefits while enabling competition.
pts.d: He proposes public compute resources to reduce competitors' capital requirements and potentially public training-data repositories subject to privacy safeguards. Infrastructure-sharing obligations could offer independent model builders terms comparable to those available to affiliated builders. His federated-learning proposal would pool learning across applications; competition would then shift toward application usability rather than underlying model intelligence. He presents these as policy options and predicted mechanisms, not demonstrated results.

pts.k: Narechania argues for early regulation of price, privacy, service quality and self-preferencing, predicting that delayed intervention becomes harder as firms gain political power.
pts.d: He treats personal-data extraction as a cost alongside developers' monetary API charges. He proposes quality standards and audits addressing bias and discrimination, with rate rules allowing continued research and development. He acknowledges that regulation might marginally slow technological development but could prevent harmful deployment. His closing comments identify privacy, quality and nondiscrimination rules as attainable interventions, with public compute also within reach; these are recommendations and qualified expectations rather than firm forecasts of enactment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily economic reasoning, prior scholarship, infrastructure analogies and hypothetical scenarios rather than empirical AI-market measurements.
pts.d: Narechania refers to his prior natural-monopoly scholarship and a coauthored anti-monopoly paper, without presenting their underlying data. He uses a stylized telephone-network cost example to explain declining average costs and compares AI governance with utility rate regulation, net neutrality, telecommunications access rules and antitrust disputes. He invokes the government's role in the internet's origins and existing data.gov repositories to support the feasibility of public resources. The transcript supplies no quantified market-share analysis, benchmark results, observed application foreclosure or measured causal effects of concentration on bias. He explicitly lacks certainty about API profitability and future model-cost estimates; the host's cost projections are not independent findings by Narechania.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source presents concentration as a current tendency and its harms as conditional future risks, with an immediate policy window but no dated forecast.
pts.d: In this source labeled 2025, Narechania urges intervention now rather than after further consolidation. His natural-monopoly argument depends on economies of scale extending across the relevant market and on pooled learning benefits; he acknowledges that scale may run out, specialized models may serve distinct uses, and geographic market boundaries remain uncertain. Outage risks depend on shared downstream reliance; chip interruption would leave existing infrastructure operating until failure while preventing future expansion. Public data proposals require privacy and compensation decisions. He recognizes uncertainty about regulation's effect on innovation and offers no numerical probability or timetable for economic harm or legislation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include model entrants, independent application developers, users, people subject to AI decisions and the public dependent on concentrated infrastructure.
pts.d: Independent model builders face capital and infrastructure-access barriers; application developers, including contract-drafting vendors, face API costs and potential disadvantages relative to affiliated products. Users face monetary costs, data extraction and service-quality risks. Job applicants and people exposed to facial recognition or criminal-justice uses may experience discriminatory outcomes; patients may be exposed to widely replicated medical-model errors. Businesses and the public relying on AI services face outages and supply-chain vulnerabilities. Incumbent model and cloud providers would face proposed access, pricing, quality or structural obligations. The interview does not make specific claims about law-firm staffing, lawyer displacement, billing models or access to civil legal help.
